summary: Describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic over a Frame Relay backbone, covering both bridging and routing. It replaces RFC 1294 and RFC 1490. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: Frame Relay is a kind of telephone company data road. This document says how to pack up different kinds of network traffic to drive along it.

subtitle: How routers and bridges wrap IP and other traffic so it can cross a Frame Relay network.

tldr.problem: A Frame Relay network carries frames over virtual circuits but has no built-in way to say which protocol is inside a frame, so a receiving router or bridge cannot tell IP from ISO CLNP from a bridged Ethernet frame.
tldr.mechanism: Every packet goes inside a Q.922 frame with a one-octet control field (UI, 0x03) and a Network Level Protocol ID (NLPID). Protocols without an NLPID use NLPID 0x80 and a SNAP header; bridged LAN frames use SNAP with OUI 0x00-80-C2.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 55) that replaces RFC 1490 and RFC 1294, and it fixes IP to the compact NLPID 0xCC form.

today: RFC 2427 is an Internet Standard (STD 55) published in September 1998. It obsoletes RFC 1490 and RFC 1294, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Frame Relay Basics
sections.content:
RFC 2427 describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic over a Frame Relay backbone. It covers both routing and bridging. It applies to end stations (DTEs) on a public or private Frame Relay network, and it does not describe how the network's own equipment (DCEs) behaves, except where a DTE must react to it.

The Frame Relay network offers virtual circuits between attached stations. Each circuit is identified at each interface by a Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI), and in most cases a DLCI only has local meaning at that interface. The rules apply to both switched and permanent virtual circuits.

A station that can use this encapsulation and others MUST know in advance which virtual circuits carry which encapsulation, and this one is only used on circuits explicitly configured for it. The RFC replaces RFC 1490 and RFC 1294.
sections.eli5: Think of Frame Relay as roads between towns. Each road has a number that only makes sense in your own town. This memo is about how to pack the trucks that drive on those roads.

sections.title: The Frame Format
sections.content:
All protocols MUST put their packets inside a Q.922 Annex A frame. The frame runs from an opening flag (0x7E) through a Q.922 address, a control field, an optional pad, the NLPID, the data, a two-octet Frame Check Sequence and a closing flag.

The Q.922 address is normally two octets and holds a 10-bit DLCI, and some networks may use three or four octets. The control field is the Q.922 control field; the UI value 0x03 is used unless negotiated otherwise, and XID (0xAF or 0xBF) is also permitted. The pad, when present, is a single octet with value zero that aligns the data to a two-octet boundary.

The NLPID is administered by ISO and the ITU and tells the receiver what protocol or encapsulation follows. The value 0x00 cannot be told apart from a pad, so it is invalid in this scheme.

There is no commonly implemented minimum for the maximum frame size. A network must support at least 262 octets, the maximum is generally 1600 octets or more, and a DTE must let its maximum acceptable frame size be configured. The smallest frame is five octets between the flags with a two-octet address.
sections.eli5: Every parcel gets the same kind of outer wrapper: a start mark, an address, a note saying what is inside, the contents and a check number at the end. The note saying what is inside is the NLPID.

sections.title: Routed and Bridged Frames
sections.content:
Two kinds of packets cross the network: routed packets and bridged packets. They have different formats, so the frame must tell the receiver which one it is. The NLPID and a SNAP header do that job.

Routed frames. Not every protocol has its own NLPID. Such a protocol is sent with NLPID 0x80 followed by a SNAP header and a pad octet. The SNAP header holds a three-octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) and a two-octet Protocol Identifier (PID). With OUI 0x00-00-00 the PID is an Ethertype. If a protocol does have an NLPID, the SNAP form can be skipped and 48 bits are saved; in that case no pad octet is used.

Bridged frames. These use NLPID 0x80 and the 802.1 OUI 0x00-80-C2. The PID says which MAC header follows (802.3/Ethernet, 802.4, 802.5, FDDI or 802.6) and whether the original LAN FCS is kept. PID 0x00-0E marks bridge protocol data units (BPDUs) and 0x00-0F marks Source Routing BPDUs. For 802.6 there is one PID, because the CIB bit in the frame says whether a CRC-32 is present.
sections.eli5: Some parcels have a standard sticker. Others need a longer label saying who made the contents. Parcels from other office networks get a special label naming which kind of office network they came from.

sections.title: Link Parameter Negotiation
sections.content:
Stations MAY support the Exchange Identification (XID) procedure of Q.922 Appendix III. It lets the two ends of a circuit agree on the maximum frame size (N201), the retransmission timer (T200) and the maximum number of outstanding information frames (K) when the circuit starts. A station that does not want acknowledged mode multiple frame operation sets K to zero.

Without XID, these values must be configured by mutual agreement or left at the Q.922 defaults given in the RFC: N201 of 260 octets, T200 of 1.5 seconds, and K of 3 for a 16 Kbps link, 7 for 64 Kbps, 32 for 384 Kbps and 40 for 1.536 Mbps or above.

A station that supports XID and receives an XID frame MUST answer with an XID response. If the remote maximum frame size is smaller than the local one, the local system reduces the size it uses to the remote value before it sends its response.
sections.eli5: Before two people start swapping boxes, they can agree how big a box may be and how long to wait for a thank-you. If they do not talk, they use the standard rules.

sections.title: Address Resolution over PVCs
sections.content:
The RFC describes address resolution only for permanent virtual circuits (PVCs); switched circuits are left to future documents. A station can use the standard ARP inside a SNAP-encoded frame with OUI 0x00-00-00 and PID 0x0806. The ARP hardware type for Frame Relay is 15 (0x000F), the hardware address length is 2, 3 or 4, and the operation codes are 1 for request and 2 for reply.

A problem is that DLCIs are local, so a station has no address of its own to put in the ARP packet. The network rewrites the DLCI as the frame crosses it, so the receiver sees the DLCI that corresponds to the sender. The receiving Frame Relay interface takes the sender hardware address from the frame header and writes it into the ARP packet. In the RFC's Figure 1, A sends on DLCI 50 and B sees DLCI 70. The target hardware address is invalid and may be zero-filled or ignored.

RARP works the same way, and the Frame Relay interface only has to act on incoming packets. Without suitable multicast, an ARP request is sent down each relevant circuit to imitate a broadcast. Inverse ARP (RFC 2390) is not required, but the RFC says it has proven useful for interface autoconfiguration.

Stations MUST be able to map more than one IP address in the same subnet to one DLCI, for uses such as remote access servers acting as ARP proxies. A station may announce a new address with an unsolicited ARP request whose source and destination IP addresses are both the new address, and the receiver MUST store the new association and remove any old one on another DLCI.
sections.eli5: Each town numbers the roads its own way, so you cannot sign your letters with your road number. The post office stamps the right number on the letter as it arrives, and the receiver reads it from the stamp.

sections.title: Carrying IP and Other Protocols
sections.content:
IP could be sent either with NLPID 0xCC or with NLPID 0x80 plus a SNAP header (OUI 0x00-00-00, PID 0x0800). The RFC picks one: IP data MUST be sent using NLPID 0xCC. That form is 48 bits shorter and matches how IP is carried over X.25.

For other protocols the rule is the same: SNAP is only used when the protocol has no NLPID. ISO CLNP has NLPID 0x81, so its packet follows directly, and the NLPID is also part of the CLNP packet itself and is not repeated. IPX has no NLPID, so it goes in a SNAP header with PID 0x8137.

For protocols with neither an NLPID nor a SNAP form, Appendix B says to use NLPID 0x08 (Q.933), followed by four octets that identify layer 2 and layer 3 protocols. It also shows how ISO 8208 uses Q.922 I frames.
sections.eli5: If your parcel type has its own standard sticker, use it, because it is smaller. Only use the long label when no sticker exists.

sections.title: Bridging Model for Frame Relay
sections.content:
Bridging follows the remote bridging model of IEEE 802.1g, with virtual ports. Remote bridges are statically configured into a remote bridge group, and a Frame Relay network used for it must have a full mesh of virtual circuits between the bridges of the group. If it is not a full mesh, the bridges must be split into several groups.

The circuits can be combined into a single virtual bridge port (the LAN view) or treated as separate ports (the point-to-point view), or both can be mixed on one interface. With one virtual port per group, the standard Spanning Tree Algorithm is enough. With more than one, an extended Spanning Tree Algorithm from IEEE 802.1g is required.

In the LAN view, broadcast frames such as BPDUs are flooded to every relevant circuit, and a bridge must learn which DLCI reaches each MAC address. Bridged packets use the Section 4 encapsulation so the receiver can learn this.
sections.eli5: A group of offices can join their local networks across the roads. Every office needs a road to every other office in its group, and the offices must avoid sending the same message around in a circle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An encapsulation protocol relies on trust: the receiver must trust that the sender identified the encapsulated protocol correctly. In general, the receiver has no way to check this, and the RFC says that this would not be desired functionality.

ARP and RARP over Frame Relay inherit the security limits of ARP. Because ARP has no authentication, there are known problems such as host impersonation, and no extra security mechanism is added for Frame Relay.
sections.eli5: The receiver just believes the label on the box. Nobody checks it, so a sender could put a wrong label on, and the memo does not add a lock.
